OUTLINE VIEW
Pretest
Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
Identify degenerative ankle arthritis based on the patient history and physical examination
findings.
Identify radiographic features of degenerative ankle arthritis and review the importance of
weight-bearing imaging studies.
Review nonsurgical treatment options for the management of degenerative arthritis.
Etiology
The most common cause of ankle arthritis is trauma. Posttraumatic arthritis may result from a
fracture (bone injury) or a chronic soft-tissue injury, such as chronic lateral ankle ligament
instability.
76% to 78% of patients with ankle arthritis have posttraumatic arthritis.

Fracture malunion
Traumatic cartilage loss
Recurrent instability
Any intra-articular fracture extension, even if nondisplaced, may induce cartilage
degradation.1
The primary trauma may result in ankle joint incongruency. Intra-articular incongruity is likely
because of asymmetric joint degradation.
10% of patients with ankle arthritis have primary osteoarthritis, which is much less common
than knee or hip arthritis.
The remaining 10% of patients with ankle arthritis have arthritis resulting from other causes
(inflammatory, secondary arthritis, osteonecrosis).
Inflammatory arthritis frequently affects the joints symmetrically. Typically, the joint is
affected in a global pattern in which the entire joint becomes arthritic and the joint remains
congruent with little deformity.
Rheumatoid arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, crystalline arthritides (gout), psoriatic arthritis,
etc.
Secondary arthritis from severe foot deformity (eg, stage 4 progressive flatfoot deformity,
severe cavovarus foot deformity)
Osteonecrosis related subchondral collapse of the tibia or talus
Other causes: Hematologic joint destruction from intra-articular bleeding and blood
breakdown products (hemophilia); postinfectious causes; neuroarthropathy, such as a
Charcot joint

Etiology
Degenerative ankle arthritis usually is posttraumatic in nature.2, 3 The ankle is a highly
constrained joint with primary stability afforded by the bony anatomy. Additional
stability is afforded by the surrounding ligamentous structures and dynamic secondary
musculotendinous stabilizers. Fracture hematoma that comes in contact with the joint
may be adequate to cause cartilage degradation and the onset of arthritis, similar to
anterior cruciate ligament tears in the knee.1 Fractures and injury may compromise
ankle cartilage markedly (Figure 1). The ankle is highly susceptible to alterations in joint
loads secondary to fracture malunion or ligamentous compromise because of the small

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002053
2/13

surface area for loading during gait. Displacement as little as a 1-mm talar shift or 3° of
abnormal external rotation in a fracture malunion may result in a 40% decrease in
contact surface area, which results in- a considerable increase in tibiotalar contact
forces, hastening the development of painful arthritis.4 Ankle arthritis develops in 13% to
54% of patients with a tibial plafond fracture, 40% of patients with a bimalleolar fracture,
adn 70% of patients with a trimalleolar fracture.5 In addition, chronic ankle instability
and ligamentous incompetency also will increase peak pressures with ambulation,
leading to increased cartilage wear and arthritis6 (Figure 2). A smaller number of
patients have primary ankle osteoarthritis or rheumatoid arthritis (Figure 3).
Figure 1 AP radiograph of a right ankle demonstrates severe joint space narrowing
consistent with posttraumatic ankle arthritis caused by a previous fracture. Note the
subtle intra-articular incongruency medially. Subchondral sclerosis of the anterolateral
distal tibia, which also is characteristic of posttraumatic arthritis, also is observed.
(Courtesy of Bethany Gallagher, MD, FAAOS, Nashville, TN.)

Patient History and Physical Examination
Symptoms
Pain with weight bearing
Stiffness
Pain with range of motion (ROM)
Swelling or deformity
Crepitus
History of trauma or repetitive inversion injury or instability of the ankle
Physical examination
A standing examination is critical to observe deformity of the ankle and hindfoot.
A gait examination likely will reveal an antalgic gait but may also reveal signs of ankle
stiffness (increased external rotation progression angle, decreased tibial progression).
Evaluate for previous surgical scars and areas of swelling.
Tenderness to palpation along the anterior ankle or within the ankle gutters is common.
C sign: Patients will make a C with their hand, placing it against the anterior ankle, indicating
pain coming from beneath the tibial articular surface.
Decreased ankle plantar flexion/dorsiflexion compared with that of the contralateral side
Complete examination will also assess the motion of the hindfoot joints which will be
important for treatment planning later
Complete examination of the extremity (neurologic, vascular, etc.) may reveal findings
consistent with other etiologies or a secondary diagnosis.

Patient History and Physical Examination
Patients with degenerative ankle arthritis are a mean of 7 years younger than those with
primary ankle osteoarthritis (58 years compared with 65 years)7 (Resource 1). Men are
affected more often than women.8 Ankle arthritis considerably impairs patient quality of
life and mobility. Patients complain of anterior ankle joint pain and pain with weight
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:49 AM
AAOS | Degenerative Ankle Arthritis
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002053
5/13

bearing and stair climbing. They exhibit decreased ROM in plantar flexion and
dorsiflexion and often have a shortened stride length, shortened cadence, and
decreased walking speed.9
Evaluating the patient in a standing position is important in assessing for lower extremity
deformity that may contribute to abnormal ankle loading and symptoms. Deformity
should be considered in the degenerative ankle joint but also with respect to the
adjacent foot and alignment of the entire lower extremity. ROM of the ankle, subtalar
joints, and transverse tarsal joints is then assessed. Normal motion of the ankle is 45° of
plantar flexion and 20° of dorsiflexion. In addition, instability of the ligamentous
components is evaluated via the anterior drawer and lateral tilt tests. After degenerative
arthritis develops, instability may be difficult to elicit because of capsular thickening,
overall onset of joint stiffness, and ankle joint crepitus. Chronic lateral ankle instability
resulting in arthritis often results in ligament incompetence but a normal anterior
drawer test. The ROM, instability, and flexibility of the deformity are important factors to
consider for treatment algorithms and to determine the feasibility of nonsurgical
management, such as bracing.
Imaging Studies
Weight-bearing radiographs
AP, lateral, and mortise views
Additional foot radiographs to assess for underlying deformity
Limb-alignment, full-length radiographs if concern for proximal contribution to the deformity
or malalignment exists
Advanced imaging studies
MRIs: Helpful if a diagnosis of osteonecrosis is suspected; additional utility to examine
adjacent joints for arthritic changes if considering surgical management.
CT scans: Helpful for surgical treatment planning but typically are not part of initial patient
evaluation and treatment unless intra-articular loose bodies or debris or fracture
malalignment is suspected
Nonsurgical Management

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002053
6/13

Medical measures are to reduce inflammation created by the arthritic joint.
Anti- inflammatory medications (NSAIDs), oral or topical
Oral steroids may be considered but are associated with more considerable adverse effects.
Injections
Image guidance substantially improves accuracy in highly constrained ankle joints
(ultrasonography or fluoroscopy).
Palpation guided accuracy may be as low as 60%.10
Corticosteroid injections are the secondary treatment therapy because a powerful anti-
inflammatory agent is delivered locally.
Also may be useful diagnostically if foot deformity or adjacent joint arthritis is present to
confirm the location of pain
Hyaluronic acid and biologic agents (platelet-rich plasma, bone marrow concentrate)
currently are under investigation and are not validated for the ankle joint.
Bracing may be effective to limit motion and irritation of the affected degenerative joint,
leading to a more normal gait. Bracing is associated with variable pain relief because irritation
from ROM will be reduced and the patient may feel more stable; however, it may not reduce
weight-bearing pain.
Taping
Ankle stabilizing orthosis sports bracing
Custom bracing
Arizona brace
Double upright brace
Dynamic ankle-foot orthosis brace
Shoe wear modifications
Rocker-bottom shoe

Nonsurgical Management
If possible, all patients with degenerative ankle arthritis should undergo a trial of
nonsurgical treatment. Nonsurgical treatment may be unachievable if the patient has an
unbraceable deformity leading to impending skin compromise or if concern for
degeneration of other joints exists because of abnormal gait mechanics. However,
patients often are prescribed a course of anti-inflammatories or steroids for pain and
are offered additional treatment options, such as intra-articular injections or bracing.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:49 AM
AAOS | Degenerative Ankle Arthritis
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002053
7/13

Care must be exercised in administering serial intra-articular steroid injections because
of the risks of skin discoloration, fat necrosis, and soft-tissue compromise, as well as
infection and elevated glucose levels in patients with diabetes mellitus.11 Hyaluronic acid
injections may relieve pain, but they are not currently approved by the FDA for the
management of the ankle; therefore, they are not covered by insurance, and they are
expensive.12 Similarly, platelet-rich plasma and stem cell therapies have shown
promising results in the ankle; however, evidence is limited, and these therapies are not
covered by insurance.13
Appropriate bracing may afford pain relief and is an important treatment option to
discuss with patients. Simple options such as heel lifts reduce pain in patients with
isolated anterior impingement symptoms. Shoe modifications, such as a stiffened sole
and rocker bottom, also may reduce ankle motion and improve gait mechanics. Braces
must fit well, without skin compromise, and control sagittal and coronal motion. A
custom leather gauntlet brace (Arizona brace) often is tolerated and successful in
improving pain.14 In addition, a newer brace has been developed to manage ankle
dysfunction and pain. The intrepid dynamic exoskeletal orthosis is a custom, ground
force reaction ankle-foot orthosis that provides stability to the ankle, subtalar joint, and
midtarsal joints (Figure 4). A dynamic posterior strut stores energy to aid ambulation
and decrease pain and has shown promise in the military population (Figure 5);
however, additional studies are necessary to determine whether a dynamic posterior
strut is worth the high cost of fabrication.15
